item.title: Key West... Where Winter Feels Very Far Away
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers ready to trade snow boots for sandals, Key West offers a distinctly different version of winter. At the southernmost point of the continental United States, the island combines warm weather, eccentric character and a year-round outdoor culture, from its signature key lime specialties and conch dishes to its festivals and waterfront traditions. Just off Duval Street, Hyatt Centric Key West Resort & Spa provides a quieter waterfront base within easy reach of the island’s energy.

The resort makes the surrounding water part of the experience, with Cook Your Catch and sunset sailing excursions departing directly from its dock. Complimentary bicycles offer another way to explore Key West at an unhurried pace, while Jala Spa brings the island indoors through treatments inspired by its tropical setting. The result is a winter escape that feels less like a retreat from the season and more like stepping completely outside of it.

The Curated Take: Key West’s appeal in winter isn’t simply that it is warm. It has a personality that makes the season feel almost beside the point. For travelers seeking a genuine change of rhythm, the combination of waterfront experiences, local food, easy cycling and the island’s unmistakable character makes Key West a particularly natural counterpoint to winter elsewhere.

item.title: When the Whales Return to Samaná Bay
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Each winter, the waters of Samaná Bay in the Dominican Republic become the stage for one of the Caribbean’s most remarkable natural spectacles. From January through March, roughly 2,500 humpback whales return to the warm tropical waters to mate and give birth, bringing an extraordinary seasonal rhythm to the bay. At Cayo Levantado Resort, a secluded retreat on its own island within Samaná Bay, guests can experience the migration through seasonal whale-watching excursions, with opportunities to observe the whales breaching, surfacing and interacting with their calves in their natural habitat.

The migration is woven into the identity of the resort itself. Its open-air wellness sanctuary, Yubarta, takes its name from the humpback whale that returns to Samaná each year. Surrounded by tropical gardens, the sanctuary is dedicated to meditation, movement, rituals and personal reflection, creating a thoughtful connection between the whales’ annual return and the idea of reconnecting with one’s own natural rhythms. Beyond the migration, winter guests can kayak and paddleboard through turquoise waters, explore the island’s tropical landscape, relax on private beaches and venture into nearby Los Haitises National Park.

The Curated Take: The most compelling aspect of winter in Samaná is that the season has its own reason for being there. The whales transform the bay for several months each year, and Cayo Levantado provides a particularly intimate vantage point from which to experience that natural cycle. Rather than simply offering warm-weather refuge, the resort becomes a base for experiencing a specific moment in the life of the destination.

item.title: A Classic Vermont Winter, From Slopes to Village Lights
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At the base of Mount Mansfield, The Lodge at Spruce Peak offers a distinctly Vermont approach to winter, combining ski-in/ski-out access with the rituals and celebrations that make the season feel bigger than the slopes. As Stowe Mountain Resort opens for ski season in November, guests can step directly into a winter itinerary that ranges from skiing and skating to snowshoeing, Nordic skiing and snow biking, with the nearly 10,000-square-foot outdoor ice rink providing another focal point in the village.

The holiday season brings its own traditions, including the return of Mistletoe’s Holiday Bar and the WhistlePig Pergolas, Holiday Retreat Weekend, a family gnome hunt and the annual Spruce Peak Lights Festival with Ice Dance International, Santa and other seasonal programming. Christmas week adds afternoon tea, holiday dining and a glow skate party, while New Year’s Eve culminates with dinner, live celebrations, fireworks and a Fire & Ice performance across Spruce Peak Village. Beyond the festivities, guests can retreat to the heated outdoor pool, The Spa at Spruce Peak or the property’s restaurants, creating a winter stay that balances time on the mountain with plenty of reasons to linger off it.

The Curated Take: The appeal of Spruce Peak is the way it turns a ski trip into a fuller winter experience. The slopes provide the adventure, but skating, fireside drinks, seasonal dining, village celebrations and longstanding holiday rituals give the stay a sense of occasion that can appeal just as much to non-skiers and multigenerational travelers.

item.title: A Hudson Valley Winter Built for the Outdoors
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
When winter settles over New York’s Hudson Valley, Mohonk Mountain House becomes a destination for experiencing the season on foot, on skis and even on ice. The 1869 Victorian castle resort sits within 40,000 acres of forest, with 85 miles of trails that take on a different character under snow. Guests can explore by snowshoe or cross-country ski, join guided winter hikes equipped with micro-spikes, or simply venture into the landscape at a slower pace.

The season also brings a distinctly recreational side to the resort. Beginning in late November, the open-air pavilion becomes an outdoor ice-skating rink surrounded by snowy mountain scenery. Guests can also try snow tubing or take part in a leisurely game of curling, an Olympic winter sport, on the resort’s ice. Together, the activities create a winter experience that extends well beyond a traditional ski weekend, with the landscape itself providing the setting for both adventure and play.

The Curated Take: Mohonk’s strength in winter is its variety. Rather than requiring guests to choose between active outdoor pursuits and more leisurely seasonal pleasures, the resort makes both part of the experience. The result is a particularly appealing Hudson Valley winter escape for families and multigenerational groups, as well as travelers who want to experience the landscape without making downhill skiing the center of the trip.

item.title: A Charleston Winter With No Snow Required
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Winter in Charleston offers a different kind of seasonal escape: cooler temperatures, fewer crowds and no snow in sight. Across the harbor from historic downtown Charleston, The Beach Club at Charleston Harbor Resort & Marina in Mount Pleasant provides a waterfront base for experiencing the Lowcountry at a quieter time of year. The 92-room boutique hotel overlooks the harbor, Arthur Ravenel Bridge and the USS Yorktown, the historic World War II aircraft carrier that creates an especially distinctive backdrop from the property’s Charleston Harbor Fish House.

The resort adds its own seasonal traditions to the waterfront setting. From Thanksgiving through mid-January, a family-friendly outdoor ice rink brings a touch of winter wonderland to the harbor, while the Oysters on the Point series returns every other week from December through March with locally steamed oysters, live music and craft beer beside the water. Together, the experiences offer a distinctly Charleston version of winter, pairing the pleasures of the season with the mild-weather appeal of the Lowcountry.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is the contrast. Charleston doesn’t need to manufacture a snowy winter experience, and The Beach Club embraces that by pairing waterfront views, local seafood and outdoor gatherings with the unexpected addition of ice skating. For travelers who want some seasonal atmosphere without giving up milder weather, it offers a playful way to experience Charleston beyond the traditional high season.

item.title: Cappadocia Takes on a More Enchanting Winter Mood
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Winter casts Cappadocia in a different light at Argos in Cappadocia, where snow-dusted valleys, ancient cave dwellings and fairy chimneys become the backdrop for a slower kind of escape. In Uçhisar, guests can begin the day with a hot-air balloon ride as the landscape catches the first light, then explore underground Anatolian villages and the surrounding valleys before returning to the property’s cave suites. A fireside picnic with mulled wine and the heated outdoor pool overlooking Pigeon Valley offer warmer ways to take in the winter landscape.

Wellness is deeply connected to local traditions here. Argos Spa, the largest cave spa in Türkiye, incorporates locally sourced healing herbs and traditional Turkish baths alongside holistic treatments designed around its philosophy of energizing, harmonizing, cleansing and indulging. After dark, guided walks beneath the full moon offer another way to experience Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, while travelers looking for more active winter pursuits can arrange skiing and lessons at nearby Erciyes Ski Center.

The Curated Take: Cappadocia is already a destination that feels almost otherworldly, but winter adds a quieter, more atmospheric dimension. At Argos, the experience is particularly compelling because wellness isn’t separated from the destination. Cave architecture, Turkish bathing traditions, local herbs, winter landscapes and even the darkness of the night sky all become part of the experience, giving a familiar wellness concept a distinctly Turkish sense of place.

item.title: An Icelandic Approach to Winter Wellness
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Hotel Rangá, winter wellness begins with embracing Iceland rather than retreating from it. Set in the countryside near Hella, the lodge provides a base for exploring some of southern Iceland’s most dramatic landscapes, from glaciers, waterfalls and ice caves to the East Rangá River. The hotel’s Live Like an Icelander experience introduces guests to local approaches to wellbeing and longevity, while more invigorating pursuits include cold plunges in the river before returning to the warmth of the hotel’s geothermal outdoor hot tubs.

Winter’s darker skies add another dimension to the experience. A Northern Lights wake-up call gives guests the chance to step outside when the aurora appears, while the property’s observatory offers nighttime stargazing with a resident astronomer. Inside, individually themed suites inspired by different continents provide a cozy retreat, and Rangá Restaurant serves Nordic cuisine to round out a day spent immersed in the landscape.

The Curated Take: The most compelling aspect of Hotel Rangá’s winter program is that wellness isn’t treated as an indoor escape from the elements. Cold water, geothermal heat, darkness, fresh air and time outdoors are all part of the experience, reflecting a distinctly Icelandic relationship with the environment. For travelers interested in wellness with a genuine sense of place, that makes the landscape itself part of the retreat.

item.title: Where Alpine Adventure Meets High-Tech Recovery
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Six Senses Crans-Montana, winter is designed around both the mountain and what happens after a day on it. Set high in the Swiss Alps with direct ski-in/ski-out access, the resort offers early access to the slopes through First Tracks, while its Gondola Awakening provides a more leisurely start, with hot drinks, energy balls and mini viennoiseries served during the ride toward the summit. At the top, guests can head onto the slopes before the crowds for an early-morning ski experience surrounded by panoramic Alpine scenery.

The resort’s winter program extends beyond skiing, with snowshoeing, winter hiking and sledding offering slower ways to experience the landscape. Recovery takes an equally prominent role back at the resort through the Ski Spa Curated Recovery experience, which includes access to a Biohack Recovery Lounge equipped with compression boots, red-light LED therapy, binaural beats and PEMF technology. New seasonal offerings include a Sensory Aufguss Ceremony and Assisted Stretch Pod, while returning guests from the mountain are welcomed with warm Alpine-essential-oil towels, herbal shots and a guided biohacking recovery session.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is the deliberate pairing of exertion and restoration. Rather than treating the spa as something separate from the ski experience, Six Senses builds recovery into the rhythm of the day, creating a winter escape where the mountain provides the adventure and the resort is designed to help guests make the most of it.

item.title: Savannah Gets an Alpine Winter Escape
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Beginning November 13, 2026, Savannah’s Lost Square rooftop will trade its usual warm-weather sensibility for an alpine-inspired winter setting. At The Alida, the hotel’s rooftop bar transforms into Alpine Village, surrounding guests with twinkling lights, private yurts and panoramic views across the Savannah skyline. Each yurt accommodates up to six guests for a private seasonal experience built around festive cocktails, winter treats and fireside s’mores.

The experience continues downstairs at The Alpine Hideaway in The Trade Room, where winter décor and warm cocktails, including Hot Toddys, extend the après-ski atmosphere. The result is a distinctly Savannah interpretation of the alpine tradition, swapping mountain slopes for rooftop views while retaining the convivial appeal of gathering around the fire with a seasonal drink in hand.

The Curated Take: Alpine winter experiences usually come with an obvious geographical requirement. The Alida’s concept is interesting precisely because it removes that requirement. In a city better known for its historic squares, Lowcountry architecture and mild winters, the seasonal transformation offers a playful reason to experience Savannah through an entirely different lens.

item.title: A Winter Retreat in the Heart of New Hampshire
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers who would rather lean into winter than escape it, Mountain View Grand Resort & Spa offers a classic White Mountains retreat in New Hampshire. Set against the mountain landscape, the historic resort provides a home base for embracing the season, with skiing, snowshoeing, winter hiking and snowy mountain scenery all close at hand.

Back at the resort, the experience shifts from outdoor adventure to cozy restoration. Guests can warm up in the indoor pool, retreat to the Tower Spa or settle into fireside spaces after a day in the cold. The combination makes winter itself part of the appeal, rather than an obstacle to a getaway, giving travelers the chance to move between the energy of the mountains and the comfort of a traditional New England resort.

The Curated Take: There is something increasingly appealing about destinations that don’t try to neutralize winter. Mountain View Grand embraces the season as a defining part of the experience, offering the kind of snowy escape where cold-weather adventure and fireside relaxation are meant to complement one another.
